title: Classification, Regression, and Clustering
learningObjectives: Distinguish classification, regression, and clustering by their outputs.
Trace model outputs into a product decision.
Choose metrics appropriate to each task.

mentalModel.text: Ask what kind of answer the system must produce. A class or category is classification. A numeric quantity is regression. A grouping discovered without predefined labels is clustering. The product's decision policy sits on top of the model output.

blocks.text: A request to “predict customer behavior” hides several different tasks. Predicting whether a customer will churn is classification; estimating how much they will spend is regression; discovering unknown behavioral groups is clustering. Define the output before choosing an algorithm.

concepts.title: Technical deep dive and worked example

blocks.text: Classification predicts categories and may return scores or probabilities. Regression estimates numeric targets. Clustering groups examples by a similarity criterion without supplied target classes. A cluster ID does not inherently mean rank or business value.

blocks.title: Task types
rows: Precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC or PR-AUC
Stability, interpretability, internal and downstream checks

blocks.problem: A delivery product returns fraud score 0.82, estimated delivery time 47 minutes, and cluster ID 2.
reasoning: Treat fraud detection as classification; a threshold or policy converts its score into action.
Treat delivery time as regression and measure error in minutes.
Treat cluster 2 as a group identifier; inspect group properties before assigning business meaning.
blocks.outcome: Output type determines the evaluation method and downstream policy.

blocks.source:
fraud_probability = 0.82
predicted_delivery_minutes = 47
cluster_id = 2
review_threshold = 0.75
send_to_review = fraud_probability >= review_threshold
print(send_to_review)
print(f"Estimated delivery: {predicted_delivery_minutes} minutes")
print(f"Discovered segment: {cluster_id}")
blocks.title: Model output versus product decision

blocks.text:
Expected output:
True
Estimated delivery: 47 minutes
Discovered segment: 2
The threshold 0.75 is illustrative, not universal. Choose it from error costs and operational capacity.

Classification thresholds trade false positives against false negatives. Regression needs error units and tail analysis. Clustering depends on feature scale, distance choice, and stability; a cluster ID is not a ranked score.
Production check: monitor false-positive review workload, regression error by region/time, and cluster stability when incoming data changes.

blocks.title: Do not confuse model output with business policy
blocks.content: A probability is not an action by itself. A cluster ID is not a label with known meaning. A regression estimate is not a guarantee.

blocks.text: 1. Problem and motivation — A product manager asks for a “prediction” without defining whether the answer should be a category, number, or discovered grouping.
2. Definition and design choice — Classification predicts a category, regression predicts a number, and clustering discovers groups without predefined target labels.
3. Internal mechanism — Classification learns class boundaries/scores; regression fits a numeric target; clustering groups rows using a distance or similarity criterion.

blocks.problem: Choose a task type for three requirements.
reasoning: Will this transaction be fraudulent? → classification.
How many minutes until delivery? → regression.
Which patterns exist in unlabeled customers? → clustering.
blocks.outcome: Write down the target/output before selecting an algorithm.

blocks.text: 4. Trade-offs and scale — Thresholds affect false alarms and missed positives. Regression errors need units and tail analysis. Clustering depends on feature scaling and distance; a cluster ID has no inherent order.
5. Anti-patterns — Using accuracy alone for rare classes, comparing regression errors without units, or interpreting cluster numbers as ranked categories.
6. Interview probes — What is the target? What metric matches business cost? What threshold triggers action? How will rare cases and subgroup failures be evaluated?

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Choose metrics to match the task
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Classification: inspect confusion matrix and class metrics. Regression: report error in target units. Clustering: assess stability, interpretability, and downstream usefulness.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.text: A model score is not a product decision. Choose thresholds and actions using business costs, risk tolerance, and operational capacity.

revisionSheet.text: Ask what kind of answer the system must produce. A class or category is classification. A numeric quantity is regression. A grouping discovered without predefined labels is clustering. The product's decision policy sits on top of the model output.
Classification → categories; regression → numeric target; clustering → discovered groups.
Choose metrics appropriate to the output and error cost.
Separate model score, threshold/policy, and final action.

questions.prompt: Predicting whether a payment is fraudulent is usually which task?
questions.explanation: The target is a category such as fraud/not fraud.

questions.prompt: Predicting delivery time in minutes is usually which task?
questions.explanation: The target is numeric, so regression is the natural framing.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude from assigning a customer to cluster 3?

options.text: They are three times more valuable than cluster 1
They belong to the group assigned identifier 3

questions.explanation: Cluster IDs are identifiers and do not inherently encode rank or meaning.

questions.prompt: What does MAE measure for a delivery-time regressor?
questions.explanation: MAE averages absolute differences in the numeric target's units.

questions.prompt: A fraud threshold of 0.5 is always the best operational cutoff.
questions.explanation: The threshold depends on calibration, prevalence, review capacity, and false-positive/false-negative costs.

questions.prompt: Clusters discovered without labels should automatically be treated as real business categories.
questions.explanation: Clusters require stability, interpretability, and downstream validation.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A product manager wants to predict future customer spend and discover behavior groups.
strongAnswerPoints: Use regression for numeric spend; classification only for a defined category.
Use clustering separately to explore unlabeled groups.
Use time-aware holdout data and inspect subgroup errors.
pitfalls: Using clustering as if it predicts a known numeric target
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would clarify the output. Predicting spend is regression, predicting a defined label is classification, and discovering unknown behavior groups is clustering. I would choose separate metrics and ensure features only use information available at prediction time.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A classifier has high accuracy but misses many fraud cases. What do you investigate?
strongAnswerPoints: Measure precision, recall, and PR-AUC as appropriate.
Choose threshold using fraud costs and review capacity.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would inspect the confusion matrix and fraud recall. If fraud is rare, majority-class predictions can achieve high accuracy. I would compare precision-recall trade-offs and choose a threshold based on missed-fraud cost and review capacity.
